Professor Ramesh Srinivasan of the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), joins the programme to discuss how sophisticated micro-targeting can compromise mobile devices without users having to click on an advertisement.

The discussion examines the wider history of Israeli-linked surveillance technology, including Pegasus spyware, and the challenges governments face in regulating powerful technology and surveillance companies.

Srinivasan argues that existing regulation is failing to protect public privacy, while the design of modern digital platforms often leaves users unaware of how their personal data is collected and tracked.

Sudan's farmers are struggling with unusually low Nile River water levels during the rainy season, as changing climate conditions and ongoing conflict put further pressure on food production.

In Khartoum, farmers Idris Bashir and Eltayeb Mohammed describe the growing physical and financial burden of irrigating their crops as the river recedes. Without the natural flooding that helps replenish farmland, they face higher costs for water, fertilisers and pesticides.

The United Nations warns that environmental pressures are worsening food insecurity for millions of people already affected by Sudan's war between the Sudanese Army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

The report also examines concerns about the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) and its potential impact on downstream water availability, amid wider regional debate over the Nile's resources.

description:
A Syrian court has sentenced 14 men over their involvement in the 2025 coastal massacres and subsequent unrest, in proceedings highlighting the continuing struggle for accountability after 14 years of civil war.

Three defendants received death sentences for inciting civil war, while two government soldiers were sentenced to 20 years in prison for murder. The trials relate to violence in Syria's coastal region, including Latakia, where mass killings left communities seeking justice.

Al Jazeera correspondent Heidi Pett reports that, although the proceedings mark a step towards accountability, many victims and their families believe too few people have been prosecuted.

Former Syrian president Bashar al-Assad, who was sentenced to death in absentia, remains in Russia. Moscow has indicated that it will not extradite him, raising further questions about whether he will face justice.

description:
In September 2025, 39-year-old Ismael Ayala-Uribe died just one month after entering California’s Adelanto ICE Processing Center.

He was one of more than 50 people to die in immigration custody during Donald Trump’s first 500 days back in office.

His family says he repeatedly complained of intense pain and asked for medical help, but received little beyond Tylenol. When he finally reached a hospital, his heart stopped within minutes.

The Trump administration is detaining record numbers of immigrants, and deaths in custody are soaring. Fault Lines investigates failures in medical care and oversight, allegations of retaliation against hunger strikers and the role of private prison companies in the rapid expansion of immigration detention.

description:
Immigration enforcement is emerging as a major political issue ahead of the US midterm elections, as rising arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) intensify debate over deportations and border security.

Al Jazeera's Phil Lavelle examines the human impact of the crackdown through the story of Cynthia Penaloza, whose sister, Jocelyn, was arrested during a traffic stop and faces deportation to Mexico.

The report cites figures indicating that nearly 75% of people detained by ICE in July had no criminal convictions. Meanwhile, Republican officials, including Tom Homan, are advocating tougher enforcement and expanded detention capacity, while Democratic voices, including Richard Gonzales, are calling for ICE to be abolished.

Polling cited in the report points to growing concerns among independent and Hispanic voters that immigration enforcement has gone too far.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Thousands of Colombians have taken to the streets to protest against President Abelardo de la Espriella's policies, raising concerns about human rights, democratic freedoms and social spending.

Trade unions, teachers and Indigenous groups have joined demonstrations opposing the government's approach to security and its proposed anti-terrorism legislation. Critics argue that new security measures could undermine the right to peaceful protest and violate constitutional protections.

The government says peaceful demonstrations are a right but insists that violence, vandalism and roadblocks will not be tolerated. While most rallies remained peaceful, some incidents of violence and clashes with police were reported.

Former presidential candidate Ivan Cepeda has criticised the administration, while protesters including Alix Lesmes say they will continue their campaign and prepare for a nationwide strike.

Al Jazeera's Alessandro Rampietti reports from Colombia.
